Text S1 Food waste composition 
The substrate used in this work is simulated FW to avoid the unnecessary effect 
of organic fractions variation on digestive efficiency. The simulated FW is composed 
by 400 g rice, 300 g cabbage, 200 g pork and 100 g tofu. These raw materials were 
firstly cooked in distilled water, and then were crushed to assure the particle size less 
than 5 mm. Finally, the crushed slurry was diluted to the volume of 2.0 L.

Text S2 Measurement of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) Production
According to Limbach, Wick, Manser, Grass, Bruinink and Stark 1, the 
intracellular ROS production was determined using 2’7’-dichlorodihydrofluorescein 
diacetate (H2DCFDA; Molecular Probes, Beyotime), which can be oxidized to 
fluorescent dichlorofluorescein (DCF) by intracellular ROS. The digestates were 
centrifuged at 10,000 r/min for 10 min, then the pellets were washed using phosphate 
buffer (0.1 mol/L, pH 7.4) and resuspended in phosphate buffer with H2DCF-DA (50 
μmol/L) and incubated in dark (35 ± 1 ℃). After 30 min, the pellets were centrifuged 
for 20 min and plated into a 96-well plate with phosphate buffer. Fluorescence 
measurements of DCF were conducted by a microplate reader ( Synergy Lx, BioTek ) 
with an excitation wavelength of 485 nm and an emission wavelength of 520 nm .

Text S4 The method of EPS extraction
EPS can be divided into soluble EPS (SEPS), loosely bound EPS (LB-EPS) and 
tightly bound EPS (TB-EPS) 2, and the sum of all forms of EPS was the total EPS. PN 
and PS are the main components of EPS, accounting for 1-60% and 40-95% of the 
total composition of EPS, respectively 3. Heat extraction method was modified to 
delaminate different EPS layers from WAS 4.The sludge suspension was first 
centrifuged for 10 min at 6000 rpm. The supernatant was collected as SEPS. Part of 
R-SEPS samples were stored and the rest were used for further extracting. The 
residual sludge in the tubes was then resuspended to the original volume with 0.05% 
NaCl, shaken horizontally at 150 rpm for 10 min under the temperature of 70 oC. The 
treated sludge was then centrifuged at 6000 rpm for 10 min to separate the solid and 
supernatant. The collected supernatant was regarded as the LB-EPS. The sludge mple 
(LB-EPS) left in the tubes was re-suspended in a 0.05% NaCl solution, then heated at 
80 oC for 30 min, and finally centrifuged at 6000 rpm for 15 min to collect the 
TB-EPS.

Text S5 Microscopy analysis
 For scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis, cell slurries were fxed with 
2.5% (v/v) glutaradehyde in phosphate-bufered saline, sequentially dehydrated with 
serial ethanol dilutions (20, 40, 60, 80, 95 and 100% (v/v) with every 10min per step). 
Te dried samples were coated with platinum and imaged using scanning electron 
microscope (SEM, Hitachi S-4800, Leica, Germany).
The presence of a carrier may create a physical barrier or provide an attachment 
point, thereby impeding or enhancing the contact of the colorant with the 
microorganisms. Therefore, in this study, sludge samples were collected for staining 
to assess the effectiveness of carriers in enhancing cell viability and optimizing 
microbial activity during anaerobic digestion after the introduction of micro-aeration. 
The cell viability of the sludge samples was stained using Live/Dead BacLight™ 
bacterial viability staining kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to the 
manufacturer’s instructions and observation using a confocal laser scanning 
microscope (CLSM) (ZEISS Axio Scan. Z1, Germany). Before the observations, the 
biofilm samples were rinsed with 50 mM PBS, then stained with a LIVE/ DEAD 
BacLight bacterial viability kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, UnitedStates) and 
incubated in the dark for 15 min, and afterward rinsed with 50 mM PBS twice to 
remove the residual fluorochrome. The biofilm was measured under the z-stack mode. 
The green and red dyes of SYTO-9 and propidium iodide were used to stain the live 
and dead cells, which could emit green and dead fluorescence, respectively. The

FISH Sample Preparation.The digested sludge samples collected from the 
reactor were immediately fixed in freshly prepared 4% paraformaldehyde solution. 
After fixation, they were washed with PBS buffer and then stored at -20℃ in a 
mixture of equal volumes of PBS buffer and 100% ethanol (maximum storage time: 6 
months). The digested sludge samples were processed using the paraffin-embedded 
sectioning technique, resulting in sections with a thickness of 8µm. Oligonucleotide 
probes specific for bacteria (FITC-labeled EUB338mix probes) and archaea 
(Cy3-labeled ARC915 probe) were used in this study. Samples were examined using 
an Olympus BX41 (Olympus, USA) epifluorescence microscope. The green (bacteria) 
and red (archaea) fluorescence signals in the three sets of images were analyzed using 
the software Image J.

Text S6 Microbial community and absolute quantitative PCR analyses
The changes in microbial community structure in different anaerobic digestion 
reactors were monitored by high-throughput sequencing of 16S rRNA genes. The 
total genomic DNA extraction from microbial communities was performed according 
to the instructions of the E.Z.N.A.® soil DNA kit (Omega Bio-tek, Norcross, GA, 
U.S.). The concentration and purity of DNA were detected by NanoDrop 2000 
( Thermo Scientific, Wilmington, USA ), and the quality of extracted genomic DNA 
was detected using 1 % agarose gel electrophoresis. PCR amplification of the V3-V4

Text S7 Detailed methods of untargeted LC-MS metabolomics
A certain mass of sample was accurately measured and ground, and the extract 
was added to the extract solution for metabolite extraction at low temperature, 
followed by centrifugation of the supernatant metabolite solvent for liquid 
chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS). UHPLC-MS/MS analyses were 
performed using a Vanquish UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher, Germany) and an 
Orbitrap Q Exactive TMHF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher, Germany) for 
UHPLC-MS/MS analysis.
Metabolites extraction
Accurately weigh 1000 ± 5 mg of sample into a 2 mL centrifuge tube and add a 6 
mm diameter grinding bead,and the metabolites extracted using a 1000 µL 
methanol:water (4:1, v/v) solution.The frozen tissue was ground in a grinding 
machine at 50 Hz for 6 minutes at -10 ℃ and ultrasound at 40 kHz for 30 min at 5℃. 
The samples were placed at -20℃ for 30min to precipitate proteins.After 
centrifugation at 13000g at 4℃ for 15min, the supernatants were carefully transferred 
to sample vials for LC-MS analysis.
Chromatographic separation and mass spectrometer analysis
Chromatographic separation of the metabolites was performed on a Thermo 
UHPLC system equipped with an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column (100 mm × 
2.1 mm i.d., 1.8 µm; Waters, Milford, USA).Mobile phase A is 95 per cent water + 5 
per cent acetonitrile (with 0.1 percent formic acid) and mobile phase B is 47.5 per 
cent acetonitrile + 47.5 per cent isopropanol + 5 per cent water (with 0.1 percent 
formic acid). The sample injection volume was 3 uL. The column temperature was 
maintained at 40℃. During the period of analysis, all these samples were stored at 
4℃.

The mass spectrometric data was collected using a Thermo UHPLC-Q Exactive 
HF-X Mass Spectrometer equipped with an electrospray ionization (ESI) source 
operating in either positive or negative ion mode.The samples were ionised by 
electrospray ionisation and the mass spectral signals were collected in positive and 
negative ion scanning modes, respectively. The data collected over the mass range 
m/z 70-1050 were acquired using data-dependent mass spectrometry (MS)/MS 
acquisition. The source parameters were as follows: spray voltage: 3500 V; capillary 
temperature: 325℃; heater temperature: 425℃.
Quality control sample setting
As a part of the system conditioning and quality control process, a pooled quality 
control sample (QC) was prepared by mixing equal volumes of all samples. The QC 
samples were disposed and tested in the same manner as the analytic samples. During 
instrumental analysis, a QC sample was inserted every 5-15 samples analysed to 
examine the stability of the entire assay.

Figure S6 Statistical analysis of metabolites extracted from D0Ⅲ, D20Ⅲ and T20Ⅲ samples (a) 
principal component analysis (PCA) and (b) partial least-squares discriminate analysis (PLS-DA) score 
plots of metabolic profiles.
The results of the principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least squares 
discriminat analysis (PLS-DA) showed that the distinction between different groups is 
significant, indicating that their metabolism are significantly different (Figure. S7a 
and b). Metabolites in AD process are mostly derived from materials produced by 
microbial activity and mediators formed by organics decomposition, with metabolites 
from both sources being powered by microbial activity 5. Therefore, the results 
showed that the carrier combined with micro-aeration changed the metabolic 
pathways within the microorganisms.

Figure S8 The classification of the differential metabolites at the "superclass" level of the HMDB 
database
The groups of differential metabolites were visualized and analyzed as volcano 
plots (Figureure S8a-c), and significant differential metabolites were screened as 393 
(T20 vs D0), 349 (T20 vs D20) and 367 (D20 vs D0), respectively. Studies have 
shown that the molecular and metabolic interactions between T20 and D0 were the 
key factors affecting the conversion of organic matter and the production of 
methanogenic metabolites during micro-aeration. The lowest number of differential 
metabolites was observed in the T20 group versus the D20 group, which may be 
related to the presence of the carrier. Moreover, it was also observed that these 
down-regulated metabolites were more numerous than the up-regulated metabolites 
(Figure S8, supporting statement). Venn diagram was used to collect significant 
differential metabolites between different digestive groups (Figure S8d). The results 
showed that there were 161 non-duplicated differential metabolites and 88 metabolites 
of differential metabolites were present in all the different control groups. The 
classification of differential metabolites in the three reactors based on the superclass
